pos: adv. (in high spirits; Haman's wife's counsel, to build the gallows and then go in merrily to the banquet)
etymology: From Old English myrge, pleasant. At Esther 5:14 it renders Hebrew sameach, glad or joyful — here the gladness of a man whose enemy is about to hang.
biblical_def:
The word appears once, and the sentence it appears in is one of the most chilling in Scripture: Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made. The counsel is precise about the order of events. Build the gallows first; get the warrant in the morning; then enjoy the dinner. Haman's wife understood that her husband's trouble was not the empire but one Jew who would not bow, and that the party would be spoiled until he was dealt with.

What follows is Scripture's most exact piece of reversal. That same night the king could not sleep and called for the chronicles; Haman came in the morning to ask for the hanging and was made to lead Mordecai through the street in the king's apparel; and by evening: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Fifty cubits, built to his own specification. The book of Esther never once names God, and every turn of it is His hand — the sleepless night, the chronicle opened at the right page, the queen's courage, the gallows standing ready. Solomon's law holds in the one story that does not mention the Lawgiver: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with mirth; with gaiety and laughter; jovially.
webster_full: MERRILY, adv. With mirth; with gaiety; with laughter; jovially; cheerfully.
MERRY, a. Gay and noisy; jovial; exhilarated to laughter; cheerful.
GALLOWS, n. An instrument of punishment, on which criminals are put to death by hanging.
BANQUET, n. A feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink.
CUBIT, n. In anatomy, the fore arm; in Scripture, a measure of length, about eighteen inches.
scriptures: Esther 5:14

Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.
Esther 7:10
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.
Proverbs 16:18
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Proverbs 15:13
A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
corruption_summary: Esther is read as a tale of coincidence or of human courage alone, when the absence of God's name in the book is the whole point of how the book teaches providence.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther never names God, and two bad readings follow from it. One treats the book as essentially secular — a court story of nerve and luck that made it into the canon by accident of national sentiment. The other over-corrects and inserts God into every verse as though the narrator had merely forgotten. The book itself does something more skilful than either: it removes the name and lets the reader watch a chain of events no one could have arranged — a sleepless night, a chronicle opened at one page, a gallows built to the wrong height for the wrong man — until the conclusion is unavoidable. Providence is demonstrated rather than asserted, which is exactly how most believers experience it.

Zeresh's counsel is worth naming for its own sake. She proposed that her husband settle a grudge before dinner so the dinner could be enjoyed, and Scripture records that the thing pleased Haman. This is what malice does to pleasure: it cannot rest while one man in the gate refuses to bow, and it will spend a fortune in timber to be able to eat in peace. The gallows fifty cubits high is the measure of how much a proud man's happiness depended on one Jew's knee, and how little was left of it when the knee stayed straight.
roots_summary: Hebrew sameach (H8056), glad; ets (H6086), a tree or gallows; mishteh (H4960), a banquet or drinking-feast.
roots_lines: Hebrew sameach (H8056) — glad, joyful; the adverb the AV renders merrily.
Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, timber; the word for the gallows Haman built.
Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — a feast, from the verb to drink; the banquets that frame the whole book.
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — pride; what Haman had, and what the proverb says goes before a fall.
Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, to overturn; the book's own word for the reversal of the ninth of Adar.
usage: “then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet” — settle the grudge, then enjoy dinner.
“And the thing pleased Haman” — four words that seal him.
“they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared” — built to his own specification.

pos: adj. (glad of heart; in Isaiah 24, the last people to stop singing when the earth is judged)
etymology: English merry + heart. At Isaiah 24:7 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning the glad of heart — the naturally cheerful, whose sighing marks how deep the judgment has gone.
biblical_def:
Isaiah 24 is the chapter sometimes called the prophet's apocalypse, a judgment not on one nation but on the earth, and it measures the disaster by the silence: The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh. Then: The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth. The prophet does not count the dead. He counts the instruments that have stopped. And the surest sign that the thing has reached bottom is that the merryhearted are sighing — the people who could always find a reason to sing have run out.

Scripture treats a glad heart as a real good, not a lesser spiritual state. A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance; a merry heart doeth good like a medicine; and the feasts of Israel were commanded celebrations with wine and music in them. So when Isaiah wants to say that a judgment is total he takes the gladness away, and when he wants to say that the story does not end there he puts it back — the same chapter closes with the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously, and two chapters later the mountain is covered with a feast of fat things. The mirth of tabrets ceases; the joy of the LORD does not, and the book knows the difference between the two.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): having a merry heart; gay of disposition; cheerful in temper.
webster_full: MERRYHEARTED, a. Having a merry heart; cheerful; gay.
MIRTH, n. Social merriment; hilarity; gaiety with laughter.
TABRET, n. A tabor; a small drum used as an accompaniment to a pipe or fife.
LANGUISH, v.i. To lose strength or animation; to pine; to droop; to fade.
SIGH, n. A single deep respiration; a long breath; the inspiration of a larger quantity of air than usual.
scriptures: Isaiah 24:7
The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh.
Isaiah 24:8
The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.
Isaiah 24:11
There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone.
Isaiah 24:23
Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.
corruption_summary: Christian gladness is confused with the mirth Isaiah says will cease, so that believers either chase the one or suspect the other, when Scripture distinguishes them plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors have made a mess of Christian joy. The first identifies it with the mirth of Isaiah 24 — a mood produced by wine, music and good circumstances — and so manufactures it in the meeting with lighting and volume, with the result that when the circumstances turn, the joy turns with them. The second, reacting, suspects gladness altogether, and produces congregations where laughter feels out of place. Scripture holds both ends: it commands feasts, says a merry heart doeth good like a medicine, and also says the mirth of the land is gone when God judges.

The difference is the source, and Isaiah 24 makes it visible by taking one away and leaving the other. The tabrets stop; the reign of the LORD of hosts in mount Zion does not. Nehemiah gives the positive form of the same thing to a congregation weeping over the law: the joy of the LORD is your strength — a gladness whose ground is outside the hearer and therefore survives the vintage failing. A Christian who has only the first kind of joy will be merryhearted until the wine mourns; a Christian who has the second will sigh honestly with Isaiah and still have something left.
roots_summary: Hebrew simchath leb (H8056 / H3820), glad of heart; toph (H8596), a tabret; anach (H584), to sigh or groan.
roots_lines: Hebrew sameach lev (H8056, H3820) — merry of heart; the phrase the AV compounds into one word.
Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, to groan; what the merryhearted are reduced to.
Hebrew toph (H8596) — a tabret, a hand drum; the first instrument to fall silent.
Hebrew masos (H4885) — exultation, mirth; the gladness of the land that is gone.
Hebrew amal (H535) — to languish, to droop; the state of the vine.

“The mirth of tabrets ceaseth” — the instruments counted rather than the dead.
“the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion” — what does not cease.

pos: adv. (with good cheer; Paul's manner before Felix, and the manner God requires in giving and in mercy)
etymology: From Old French chiere, the face or countenance, from Late Latin cara. At Acts 24:10 it renders Greek euthumoteron, more cheerfully — a comparative, of a prisoner answering a charge.
biblical_def:
Paul is on trial at Caesarea before Felix, with Tertullus the orator having just finished a polished indictment, and his opening words set the tone for everything after: Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself. The Greek is a comparative — more cheerfully — and the reason he gives is that the judge knows the country and will therefore be able to check the facts. A man with nothing to hide can afford good cheer in a courtroom, and Paul says a few verses later what makes it possible: herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.

The New Testament asks for the same manner in two other places where it is much harder. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver — the Greek is hilaros, from which we get hilarious, a word for a man glad to be doing it. And Romans: he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness. Both commands go behind the act to the face. God is not indifferent to whether a gift is given gladly or squeezed out, and mercy shown with a sigh is not the mercy He asks for. The standard is set by the Giver Himself, who giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with cheerfulness; with alacrity or willingness; readily.
webster_full: CHEERFULLY, adv. With cheerfulness; readily; with alacrity; willingly.
CHEERFUL, a. Lively; animated; having good spirits; full of good hope and moderate joy.
ALACRITY, n. Cheerfulness; gaiety; sprightliness; more usually, a cheerful readiness or promptitude to do some act.
GRUDGINGLY, adv. Unwillingly; with discontent or reluctance.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
scriptures: Acts 24:10

Then Paul, after that the governor had beckoned unto him to speak, answered, Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself:
Acts 24:16
And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Romans 12:8
Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.
corruption_summary: Cheerfulness is counterfeited as a required Christian face, so that a believer under real grief is made to perform a mood Scripture never asked him to fake.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a pressure in many congregations to look well, and it produces a cheerfulness that is a costume. Scripture never asks for that. Paul was cheerful in court because his conscience was clear, not because cheer was expected of prisoners, and the same man wrote that he was sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing and that within were fears. The cheerful giver of 2 Corinthians 9 is hilarious about it because he purposed it in his heart beforehand — the gladness follows a settled decision, not a demand from the platform. Cheerfulness commanded without a ground is just another weight on people already carrying one.

The commands themselves must not be softened on that account. God loves a cheerful giver, and the alternatives Paul names — grudgingly, or of necessity — are precisely how a great deal of Christian giving is actually done. The remedy Paul offers is not exhortation but a fact: ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. A man who has understood that transaction has the only durable reason to be glad about a cheque, and a man who has not will need to be squeezed every time.
roots_summary: Greek euthumos (G2115), of good cheer; hilaros (G2431), cheerful, glad; hilarotes (G2432), cheerfulness.
roots_lines: Greek euthumoteron (G2115) — more cheerfully; Paul's comparative before Felix.
Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful, merry; God loveth a cheerful giver, and the root of our hilarious.
Greek hilarotes (G2432) — cheerfulness; the manner required of him that sheweth mercy.
Greek lupe (G3077) — grief, sorrow; not grudgingly is literally not out of grief.
Greek aproskopos (G677) — without offence, not causing stumbling; Paul's conscience in Acts 24:16.
usage: “I do the more cheerfully answer for myself” — good cheer in a courtroom, on a clear conscience.
“God loveth a cheerful giver” — the face behind the gift.
“he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness” — mercy without a sigh.

pos: adv. (with joy; used of a marriage, a conversion, and the confiscation of a Christian's goods)
etymology: From Old French joie, from Latin gaudium. In the AV it renders Hebrew ra'ah chayyim at Ecclesiastes 9:9 (literally see life) and Greek chairo in the New Testament.
biblical_def:
The three places the adverb falls are worth putting side by side. Solomon: Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity... for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun. Luke, of Zacchaeus in the tree: And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. And Hebrews, of a persecuted congregation: ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods. A marriage, a conversion, and a confiscation — and the same word covers all three.

The third is the one that explains the other two, because the writer gives the reason: knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance. They could watch their property carried off gladly because they had appraised what they still had. That is the structure of Christian joy everywhere in the New Testament: it is never a denial of the loss but a comparison of it with something weightier. Peter says the same to a church under fire — rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings. And Solomon's counsel about the wife belongs in the same frame rather than against it. Ecclesiastes has just finished proving that everything under the sun is vanity; the command to live joyfully with the wife thou lovest is not escapism but the right use of a real gift held with an open hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with joy; gladly; with pleasure and satisfaction.
webster_full: JOYFULLY, adv. With joy; gladly; with satisfaction and pleasure.
JOYFUL, a. Full of joy; very glad; exulting.
SPOILING, n. The act of plundering; robbery; waste; the seizure of goods.
SUBSTANCE, n. Goods; estate; means of living; that which is real and permanent.
PORTION, n. A part of anything separated from the whole; that which is allotted.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:34
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
Luke 19:6
And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully.
Ecclesiastes 9:9

Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun.
1 Peter 4:13
But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.
corruption_summary: Joy is treated as a feeling to be sustained rather than a conclusion to be drawn, so that a Christian who is not feeling it concludes that something is wrong with his faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 10:34 gives the anatomy of Christian joy in one sentence, and it is not a mood: they took the spoiling of their goods joyfully knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance. The gladness rests on a piece of knowledge, held consciously, about what they still owned. That is why the New Testament can command joy, which would be absurd if joy were a feeling — nobody can be ordered to feel. What can be ordered is the reckoning: count it all joy, know that the trying of your faith worketh patience, remember the enduring substance.

This also disposes of the counterfeit that treats joy as evidence of a comfortable life. Every New Testament passage on the subject is set against a hard background — bonds, spoiling, fiery trial, the sufferings of Christ. Zacchaeus received Him joyfully while the whole town murmured that Jesus had gone to be guest with a sinner. The joy is not the absence of the trouble; it is the weight of the other thing in the scale, and a believer who is not feeling it is usually not commanded to feel differently but to look again at what he has.
roots_summary: Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice; chara (G5479), joy; harpage (G724), the plundering or spoiling of goods.
roots_lines: Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, to be glad; the verb behind joyfully in Luke and Hebrews.
Greek harpage (G724) — seizure, plundering; the spoiling of the Hebrews' goods.
Greek huparxis (G5223) — substance, possession; the better and enduring one in heaven.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know; the participle on which the whole joy rests.
Hebrew ra'ah chayyim (H7200, H2416) — to see life; the idiom behind live joyfully in Ecclesiastes.
usage: “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” — joy as an appraisal, not a mood.
“received him joyfully” — Zacchaeus down out of the tree.
“Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest” — a real gift, open-handed.

pos: adv. (with courage; Jehoshaphat's charge to the judges he appointed over Judah)
etymology: From Old French corage, from Latin cor, the heart. At 2 Chronicles 19:11 it renders a Hebrew verb from chazaq, to be strong, to take firm hold.
biblical_def:
Jehoshaphat has set judges through the cities of Judah and is briefing them, and the charge ends: And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king's matters: also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good. The word is the same root as the charge to Joshua at the Jordan. A judge needs courage because a judge is the one man in the room who will be hated by whoever loses, and Jehoshaphat had already told them what to hold on to: Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart, and, earlier, ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment.

Notice the structure he set up. Spiritual matters to the chief priest, civil matters to the ruler of the house of Judah, with Levites as officers — distinct jurisdictions under one God, a very early form of the principle that church and magistrate have different spheres and neither may swallow the other. And notice the promise attached to the command: the LORD shall be with the good. That is the same assurance given to Joshua — be strong and of a good courage... for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest — and it is the only ground of courage Scripture ever offers. Biblical courage is not a quality of temperament but a conclusion drawn from a Presence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with courage; boldly; bravely; with resolution and firmness.
webster_full: COURAGEOUSLY, adv. With courage; bravely; boldly; stoutly.
COURAGE, n. Bravery; intrepidity; that quality of mind which enables men to encounter danger and difficulties with firmness.
JUDGE, n. A civil officer who is invested with authority to hear and determine causes.
UPRIGHT, a. Erect; perpendicular; also, honest; just; adhering to rectitude.
DISMAYED, pp. Deprived of courage; daunted; discouraged.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 19:11

And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king's matters: also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good.
2 Chronicles 19:9
And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.
Joshua 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
1 Corinthians 16:13
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
corruption_summary: Courage is treated as a personality trait rather than a duty commanded with a promise, and the judge who fears the wrong face is excused as merely cautious.
corruption_paragraphs: Every command to courage in Scripture is attached to a fact about God, never to an assessment of the man. Joshua is told to be strong and of a good courage for the LORD thy God is with thee; Jehoshaphat's judges are told to deal courageously and that the LORD shall be with the good; Paul tells the Corinthians to quit themselves like men in the middle of a paragraph about standing fast in the faith. Courage in the Bible is therefore a duty and not a temperament, and the naturally bold have no advantage in it — Peter was bold in the garden and a coward in the courtyard within the hour.

The specific application Jehoshaphat makes deserves attention in an age when institutions bend. A judge without courage is worse than no judge, because the form of justice remains while its substance is sold to whoever can make the most trouble. The charge given to these men — ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment — is the only thing that has ever made a bench honest. Where the fear of God is gone from a courtroom, an elders' meeting or a household, what fills the gap is the fear of the loudest person present.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to take hold; amats (H553), to be alert and courageous; yare (H3372), to fear.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be firm, to strengthen; the verb behind deal courageously.
Hebrew amats (H553) — to be alert, bold; joined with chazaq in the charge to Joshua.
Hebrew yirath YHWH (H3374) — the fear of the LORD; the disposition Jehoshaphat required of his judges.
Hebrew shalem (H8003) — whole, perfect; with a perfect heart.
Greek andrizomai (G407) — to act like a man; Paul's quit you like men.
usage: “Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good” — a command with a promise attached.
“Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD” — the only thing that keeps a bench honest.
“quit you like men, be strong” — Paul's version, set beside standing fast in the faith.

pos: adj. (from the heart; of the counsel a friend gives, which Solomon compares to ointment and perfume)
etymology: From Old English heorte, the heart. At Proverbs 27:9 it renders Hebrew nephesh, the soul — counsel out of a man's soul, not off the top of his head.
biblical_def:
Solomon puts friendship beside the two most expensive pleasant things in his world: Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel. The Hebrew for hearty is nephesh, soul — counsel from the soul. It is the difference between advice and a friend. Anyone can supply an opinion; what Solomon praises is the man who gives you what he actually thinks, out of who he is, because he loves you and will still be there afterwards.

Eight verses later comes the line that shows what such counsel costs: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. Iron on iron makes sparks and takes metal off both blades. Proverbs has no category for a friendship that never abrades. The same chapter says faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful — wounds from the friend, kisses from the enemy, and the reader is told which to prefer. The New Testament carries the word over into the whole of a Christian's work: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. Hearty in Scripture never means loud or hail-fellow. It means proceeding from the soul, and it is the difference between a man's service and his performance as much as between his friendship and his politeness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): proceeding from the heart; sincere; warm; cordial; not feigned.
webster_full: HEARTY, a. Proceeding from the heart; sincere; warm; zealous; cordial.
HEARTILY, adv. From the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity; really; truly.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.
OINTMENT, n. Unguent; any soft unctuous substance used for smearing, particularly the body or a diseased part.
SINCERE, a. Pure; unmixed; being in reality what it appears to be; not feigned.
scriptures: Proverbs 27:9
Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
Proverbs 27:17
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Proverbs 15:13
A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
corruption_summary: Friendship has been redefined as unconditional affirmation, which removes from it the one thing Proverbs says a friend is for.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing account of a good friend is someone who supports you in whatever you have decided. Proverbs 27 describes something else entirely: a man who sharpens your countenance the way iron sharpens iron, whose wounds are faithful, and whose counsel comes out of his soul rather than out of his instinct to keep the peace. On the modern definition, the friend who says the hard thing has broken the friendship by saying it. On the biblical definition, he has just performed its central service, and the enemy is the one whose kisses are plentiful.

The corresponding abuse must also be named, because a certain kind of blunt Christian quotes Proverbs 27:6 as a licence to be unpleasant. Faithful are the wounds of a friend assumes a friend — someone who has earned the right by long, costly loyalty, whose counsel is sweet like ointment before it is sharp like iron. A stranger's correction is not a faithful wound; it is a wound. What makes hearty counsel bearable is that it comes from a man whose love is not in question, which is why Paul could write 1 Corinthians and still be received by them.
roots_summary: Hebrew nephesh (H5315), the soul; etsah (H6098), counsel; chadad (H2300), to sharpen; Greek ek psuches (G1537 / G5590), from the soul.
roots_lines: Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, self; hearty counsel is counsel out of the soul.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; the gift Solomon compares to ointment.
Hebrew chadad (H2300) — to be sharp, to sharpen; iron upon iron.
Hebrew metheq (H4986) — sweetness; what a friend's counsel is to the heart.
Greek ek psuches (G1537, G5590) — from the soul; Paul's heartily at Colossians 3:23.
usage: “the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel” — counsel out of the soul.
“Iron sharpeneth iron” — sparks, and metal off both blades.
“do it heartily, as to the Lord” — service, not performance.

pos: n. (agreeableness; the quality of wisdom's ways in Proverbs 3)
etymology: From Old French plaisant, from Latin placere, to please. At Proverbs 3:17 it renders Hebrew noam, pleasantness or beauty — the same word in let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us.
biblical_def:
Solomon is describing wisdom as a woman worth more than rubies, and gives her two roads: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. The Hebrew noam means agreeableness, loveliness, and is the same word in the psalm that asks that the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us. Wisdom is not being commended here as effective or prudent, though Proverbs says that elsewhere. She is commended as pleasant — the life lived her way is a better life to live, not merely a safer one.

This needs saying because the moral vocabulary of Scripture is often heard as pure restriction. Proverbs 3 does not begin the description with warnings; it begins with Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and continues to the length, riches, honour, pleasantness and peace that follow her. The Psalter says the same of God Himself in a sentence that outruns every rival offer: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. The Christian doctrine of pleasure is not that pleasure is dangerous but that it is God's, that He has more of it than sin does, and that He keeps it longer. Moses is commended in Hebrews for choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, and the phrase that decides it is the last three words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the quality of being pleasant; agreeableness; that which gives pleasure or delight.
webster_full: PLEASANTNESS, n. State of being pleasant or agreeable; cheerfulness; gaiety; that quality which gives pleasure.
PLEASANT, a. Pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses.
PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track; a course of life or conduct.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation.
DELIGHT, n. A high degree of pleasure or satisfaction of mind; joy.
scriptures: Proverbs 3:17
Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.
Proverbs 3:13
Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding.
Psalm 16:11
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Ecclesiastes 9:9

Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun.
corruption_summary: Holiness is presented as the surrender of pleasure, and the world is left holding a monopoly it does not own.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of preaching has conceded the central point before the argument starts, by presenting the Christian life as the renunciation of enjoyment in exchange for a reward later. Proverbs 3 says wisdom's ways are pleasant now; Psalm 16 says fulness of joy is where God is; and the Lord Jesus said He came that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly. The Puritans, who are caricatured on this point more than any other body of Christians, wrote some of the warmest material in English on the enjoyment of God — Burroughs on contentment, Sibbes on the bruised reed, Watson on the beatitudes. The catechism's first answer is not to obey God and endure Him for ever.

The qualification Scripture insists on is not that pleasure is bad but that sin's pleasures are short. Hebrews grants that there were pleasures in Egypt and says Moses weighed them: he chose affliction with the people of God rather than the pleasures of sin for a season, having respect unto the recompence of the reward. That is an argument from arithmetic, not from asceticism. A believer who has genuinely tasted that the Lord is good is not making a sacrifice when he turns from what is on offer; he is declining the worse of two pleasures, and Proverbs 3:17 tells him plainly which road is the agreeable one.
roots_summary: Hebrew noam (H5278), pleasantness, beauty; shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness; naim (H5273), pleasant.
roots_lines: Hebrew noam (H5278) — pleasantness, agreeableness, beauty; also the beauty of the LORD in Psalm 90:17.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, completeness, welfare; wisdom's other road.
Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a path, a beaten track; the word rendered paths.
Hebrew esher (H835) — blessedness, happiness; happy is the man that findeth wisdom.
Hebrew naim (H5273) — pleasant, delightful; used of brethren dwelling together in unity.
usage: “Her ways are ways of pleasantness” — wisdom commended as agreeable, not merely safe.
“in thy presence is fulness of joy” — where the pleasures actually are.
“the pleasures of sin for a season” — the three words that decide the arithmetic.

pos: adj. (delightful; of the land Malachi promises to a people who bring in the tithes)
etymology: From Old French delit, from Latin delectare, to delight. At Malachi 3:12 it renders Hebrew chephets, delight or desire — a land that is God's own pleasure.
biblical_def:
Malachi's last promise to a robbing nation is a picture of what obedience would look like from the outside: And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts. The Hebrew word is chephets, delight — the same root used of what God Himself takes pleasure in. The promise stands at the end of the paragraph that begins with the charge Will a man rob God? and the command Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, with the one invitation to testing in all Scripture: prove me now herewith.

The land itself had always been described this way. Deuteronomy calls it a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills, and Israel's tenure in it was always covenantal — not a possession but a stewardship, held on terms, with the tithe as one of the standing signs that the Owner had not sold the freehold. Malachi's charge is that the nation had begun treating God's portion as its own, and the promise is that a people who stopped doing so would become something the nations noticed. The word is worth keeping for what it says about God's aim: He does not merely intend His people to be obedient. He intends them to be delightsome.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): very pleasing; delightful; affording great pleasure or satisfaction.
webster_full: DELIGHTSOME, a. Very pleasing; delightful.
DELIGHT, n. A high degree of pleasure or satisfaction of mind; joy.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.
STOREHOUSE, n. A house in which things are stored; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
BLESSED, a. Happy; prosperous in worldly affairs; enjoying spiritual happiness and the favor of God.
scriptures: Malachi 3:12
And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.
Malachi 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
Deuteronomy 8:7
For the LORD thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills;
2 Corinthians 9:8
And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:
corruption_summary: Malachi 3:10 has been turned into a transaction — give and God is obliged to pay — which empties both the covenant it belongs to and the God it names.
corruption_paragraphs: Few verses have been more abused on television than prove me now herewith. Lifted out of Malachi, it becomes a formula: deposit, and heaven is contractually bound to return more. Several things are wrong at once. The promise is addressed to a national covenant people under Mosaic law, whose tithe supported a temple and a priesthood, in a land held on covenant terms; the blessing named is agricultural, rain and harvest in a specific country; and the whole charge is that they had been robbing God, not that they had found the key to prosperity. A promise given to a nation for restitution is not a mechanism for private enrichment.

What survives into the New Testament, and survives fully, is the principle that God is no man's debtor and gives with an open hand to those who give with one. Paul's version is 2 Corinthians 9: he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully, and God is able to make all grace abound toward you — and note what the abundance is for, that ye may abound to every good work, not that ye may abound. The prosperity reading stops the verse a clause early. The end God has in view is a people so supplied that they can be generous, and a land the nations call delightsome because of how its people live.
roots_summary: Hebrew chephets (H2656), delight, desire; maaser (H4643), a tithe; bachan (H974), to test or prove.
roots_lines: Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight, pleasure, that in which one takes joy; the land God would delight in.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tenth, a tithe; brought into the storehouse for the house of God.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to prove; prove me now herewith.
Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasury, a storehouse; the temple chambers where the tithe was kept.
Hebrew ashar (H833) — to call blessed, to pronounce happy; what all nations would do.
usage: “ye shall be a delightsome land” — God's aim is not merely obedience.
“prove me now herewith” — the one invitation to testing in Scripture, and its context.
“that ye may abound to every good work” — the clause the prosperity reading omits.

pos: n. (liberality; the open-handedness Paul says the Corinthians' supply will be enriched unto)
etymology: From Old French bonte, goodness, from Latin bonitas. At 2 Corinthians 9:11 it renders Greek haplotes, singleness or simplicity — a heart without a second motive, and so open-handed.
biblical_def:
Paul is organizing the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and he states the purpose of the enrichment he prays for: Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God. The preposition carries the argument. They are enriched to bountifulness — the increase is for the giving, and the giving is for the thanksgiving, and the thanksgiving is God's. Nothing in the chain stops at the Corinthians, and Paul never once suggests it should.

The Greek word is haplotes, which means singleness — a heart with one motive rather than two. The same noun is what Romans 12 requires of the man who gives: let him do it with simplicity. Generosity in the New Testament is defined less by amount than by undividedness, which is why the widow's two mites outweighed the rest of the treasury. The chapter's governing law is stated in agricultural terms — he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully — and its ground is stated in the previous chapter in the plainest sentence on the incarnation and giving in the Bible: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. Christian bountifulness is not generosity as a virtue; it is imitation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): liberality in bestowing gifts; munificence; generosity.
webster_full: BOUNTIFULNESS, n. The quality of being bountiful; liberality in bestowing gifts and favors.
BOUNTIFUL, a. Free to give; liberal in bestowing gifts and favors; munificent; generous.
BOUNTY, n. Liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
SIMPLICITY, n. Singleness; the state of being unmixed or uncompounded; artlessness of mind; freedom from duplicity.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 9:11
Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God.
2 Corinthians 9:6
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
2 Corinthians 8:9
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
corruption_summary: The sowing-and-reaping language of 2 Corinthians 9 is preached as an investment scheme, and the verse that names the purpose of the increase is left out.
corruption_paragraphs: He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully is read as a return on capital, and the reading requires ignoring the next five verses. Paul says the increase is to all bountifulness, that its effect is thanksgiving to God, that the ministration supplies the want of the saints and abounds by many thanksgivings, and that the recipients will glorify God for the professed subjection of the givers to the gospel of Christ. Every clause points outward and upward. The giver is not the terminus of anything in the chapter, and a teaching that makes him the terminus has inverted it.

The word itself supplies the corrective. Haplotes is singleness, a motive not divided in two, and a gift given in order to receive is by definition double-minded. This is why Paul grounds the whole appeal not in return but in the Lord Jesus, who, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor. Nothing came back to Him from the Corinthians; the whole transaction ran one way, and it is the pattern. Christian generosity is at its root an imitation of an act that expected no repayment, and the reaping Paul promises is real precisely because it is not the reason.
roots_lines: Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, simplicity, and so liberality; rendered bountifulness.
Greek ploutizo (G4148) — to make rich; being enriched in every thing.
Greek eucharistia (G2169) — thanksgiving; the end of the whole chain.
Greek eulogia (G2129) — a blessing, and so a bountiful gift; Paul's word for the collection itself.
Greek ptocheuo (G4433) — to become poor as a beggar; what the Lord Jesus did in 2 Corinthians 8:9.
usage: “enriched in every thing to all bountifulness” — the preposition carries the doctrine.
“which causeth through us thanksgiving to God” — where the chain ends.
“though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” — the pattern, not the investment.

pos: adv. (freely, without stint; of the master furnishing a freed servant, and of God giving wisdom)
etymology: From Latin liberalis, befitting a free man, from liber, free. At Deuteronomy 15:14 it renders a Hebrew verb meaning to lade or garland; at James 1:5, Greek haplos, singly, without reserve.
biblical_def:
Two uses, one in each Testament, and together they are a small theology of giving. The first is the law of release: in the seventh year a Hebrew servant goes free, and Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him. The Hebrew verb means to garland or load up — hang gifts on him. The man has served six years and is owed nothing further, and the master is commanded to send him away loaded, from all three sources of his own living, for a reason stated a few verses later: thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee.

The second is James: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him. The Greek is haplos, singly, without a second thought — and then the clause that removes the last excuse for not asking: and upbraideth not. God does not remind the asker that he has been here before, or that he should have known better, or that he wasted the last supply. Every human benefactor eventually upbraids. The one being appealed to in James 1 does not, and that is what makes the asking possible for a man who has already made a mess of things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): bountifully; freely; largely; with munificence; without stint.
webster_full: LIBERALLY, adv. Bountifully; freely; largely; with munificence.
LIBERAL, a. Generous; bountiful; munificent; not selfish, narrow or contracted.
UPBRAID, v.t. To charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach; to chide; to reprove with severity.
FURNISH, v.t. To supply with anything necessary, useful or ornamental; to provide.
BONDMAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages.
scriptures: James 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
Deuteronomy 15:14
Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him.
Deuteronomy 15:10

Thou shalt surely give him, and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him: because that for this thing the LORD thy God shall bless thee in all thy works, and in all that thou puttest thine hand unto.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
corruption_summary: Generosity is thought of as a temperament some people have, when Scripture commands it, regulates the heart behind it, and grounds it in redemption from Egypt.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 15 is remarkable for legislating an emotion. It does not merely command the gift — thou shalt surely give him — it adds and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him, which is the Old Testament's form of God loveth a cheerful giver. And it supplies the motive: remember that thou wast a bondman, and the LORD redeemed thee. Christian generosity has exactly the same structure. It is commanded, it is a matter of the heart and not only the hand, and its ground is a redemption the giver received without earning. A man who thinks of himself as naturally ungenerous has not been excused; he has been told where to look.

The New Testament use adds what is perhaps the most pastorally valuable clause in James. God giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not. The second half is why the first can be believed. Most of us know what it is to ask a second time and be given the help along with the reminder of how we came to need it. The believer who has squandered wisdom, gone his own way, and come back empty is told that the Giver will not upbraid him — and it is precisely because giving is God's single-minded nature, not a favour extracted from Him, that the asking may be done without shame.
roots_summary: Hebrew anaq (H6059), to garland or lade with gifts; Greek haplos (G574), singly, liberally; oneidizo (G3679), to upbraid.
roots_lines: Hebrew anaq (H6059) — to encircle as with a necklace, to load with gifts; furnish him liberally.
Greek haplos (G574) — singly, without reserve or second motive; how God gives.
Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach, to upbraid; what He does not do.
Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom; the thing James invites the lacking to ask for.
Hebrew ra'a levav (H7489, H3824) — to be grieved of heart; what Deuteronomy forbids in the giver.
usage: “that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” — the clause that makes asking possible.
“Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock” — a freed man sent away loaded.
“thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest” — an emotion under law.
